newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe rushes to settle truck strike.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe rushes to settle truck strike.

text.p: The French government raced against time on Tuesday to settle a nine-day-old truck drivers' strike strangling France's highways and fuel supplies before it spreads to other sectors in a re-run of last year's labour crisis.
Foreign governments put pressure on Paris to guarantee freedom of movement on roads choked by some 180 roadblocks.

British Prime Minister John Major warned the French they could face compensation claims and the International Road Transport Union (IRU) in Geneva urged Paris to end the blockage of foreign traffic passing through the country.

The dispute began to hit the franc on foreign exchange markets. The currency lost ground against the dollar and the mark as traders, recalling last year's damaging 24-day public transport strike, weighed the risk of wider unrest.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe faced calls in parliament from opposition Socialists and Communists, and from some government backbenchers, to bring an early end to the dispute.

But while rushing to broker a deal between the truckers and their employers, the centre-right government was wary of setting a precedent on pay or early retirement that could whet appetites among other workers during a period of budget austerity.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said the cabinet was doing its utmost to help reach a deal and would take responsibility for easing earlier retirement for drivers and reducing payroll taxes for employers.

"The negotiations must be concluded within 24 hours," Labour Minister Jacques Barrot told a news conference. "I would be very dismayed if ulterior motives led some people to bet on a failure of these negotiations."

Barrot did not say whom he meant, but ministers were worried about threats by Force Ouvriere (FO) trade union leader Marc Blondel, the man who spearheaded last year's strike, to extend the truckers' dispute to other transport sectors.

Communist CGT union leader Louis Viannet also spoke of widening the conflict to other sectors, saying in a television interview: "It is in the truckers' interest to exert the maximum pressure, to make the employers understand that they will gain nothing by digging in their heels."
But France's biggest union, the Socialist-led CFDT, argued against spreading the dispute, saying the truckers could forfeit widespread public support.

Rail workers' unions urged members to back the truckers "by all appropriate means". But the divided unions have failed to mobilise public employees for major strikes despite repeated efforts since September.

French airline pilots' unions have called a two-day strike over terms of employment for Wednesday and Thursday. Air France said it expected to run two-thirds of its normal flights and domestic subsidiary Air France Europe said it would run half of its daily schedule.

Road haulage bosses, who complain of severe pressure on delivery times from clients and fierce competition from European rivals, were taking a hard line on the central issues of pay and hours, officials and union representatives said.

The marathon talks resumed in mid-afternoon after official mediator Robert Cros put forward government proposals to reduce social charges on employers who cut working hours and facilitate early retirement in return for the recruitment of young drivers.
The government has also pledged to ban all trucks from French roads on Sundays, a measure that previously did not apply to foreign trucks in transit.

The drivers are demanding retirement at 55 instead of the legal norm of 60, a 10 percent pay rise and a cut in working hours, as well as payment for loading time and compulsory rest periods while on the road.

The risk for the government is that sanctioning pay rises or conceding retirement at 55 would lead to demands from other unions and raise pressure from car manufacturers who are seeking state aid to cut 40,000 jobs through early retirement.

While the cost of such moves might not have much immediate impact on the budget -- French media estimates range from one to two billion francs ($200-400 million) for the truckers -- they would add to France's long-term problems in financing pensions while remaining economically competitive.
